title: Bring me your mind
hookLine: Huike asks Bodhidharma to put his mind at peace; Bodhidharma says, bring it here

lines: A MONK WHO WON'T TURN AROUND.
cards: Snow is falling. A man stands outside a monastery, waiting. Inside, the monk he has come to see sits facing a wall and doesn't turn around.
The man is Huike. He has come a long way with one trouble, the kind that follows a person from room to room. When at last he speaks, he doesn't ask a clever question.
He says: my mind isn't at peace. Please, teacher, settle it for me.

teach.h: MY MIND IS NOT AT PEACE.
teach.b: First, the request. The Gateless Gate, a collection of Chan stories with short comments, tells this as one of its cases.
Huike's words are simple enough for anyone to say at three in the morning: my mind is not at peace; please pacify it. Second, the answer. Bodhidharma doesn't offer advice or a technique.
He says: bring me your mind, and I'll pacify it for you. Hand it over. Put it on the table.

teach.h: I'VE SEARCHED AND CAN'T FIND IT.
teach.b: Huike looks, and says: I've searched for my mind, and I can't find it. Bodhidharma answers: there, I have pacified it for you. That's the whole exchange.

Chan remembers Huike as the student who received Bodhidharma's teaching, the second ancestor in its line. Fourth, what happened in that search. Huike was asked to do something odd: not to fix his mind, but to find it.
When you go looking for the anxious mind, you find things: a thought about tomorrow, a tight feeling in the chest, a picture of someone's face, a sentence repeating itself. But they keep moving.
You can't pick the whole thing up and hand it to anyone. Some readers hear Bodhidharma saying the trouble was never a solid object; others hear a teacher simply turning a student around to look.
Either way, the peace in the story doesn't come from a new answer. It comes from looking straight at the question.

how: Chan and Zen students study the exchange between Bodhidharma and Huike as a koan, and meditation teachers in several traditions invite students to turn and look directly at the mind that worries.

o: the student who couldn't find his anxious mind
the emperor who asked about his merit
the monk who wrote the first Chan rules

games.q: bring me your mind: tap the pairs.
p: my mind is not at peace

s: Bodhidharma gave Huike a breathing technique
he told him to bring his mind, so Huike went looking for it.
Huike says he searched for his mind and couldn't find it
and Bodhidharma says: there, I've pacified it for you.
Chan remembers Huike as its second ancestor
the student who received Bodhidharma's teaching.

games.q: you're Huike. you've waited in the snow, and the teacher says: bring me your mind. what do you do?
o: go looking for the mind itself.
games.why: Huike looked, and said he couldn't find it. Bodhidharma said: there, I have pacified it for you.

practice: Bring up one small worry, not the biggest one, and gently go looking for the mind that's worried: is it in the head, the chest, does it have a shape or an edge?
Each time you find a thought, notice it's already moving, and look again. If the worry softens, let it; if not, keep looking with curiosity.

wordCard.voice: Huike. The student who asked Bodhidharma to pacify his mind, and found, when he looked for it, that he couldn't.

orig.note: Chinese: an xin, peace of mind, the word in Huike's request.

carryVoice: Your line: I can't find it. A worry looked at closely keeps on moving. That's day nine hundred thirteen.
